title: SBI PO Pre — Mock Test 1
description: Full-length 100-question mock test simulating the latest SBI PO Prelims pattern. Sectional timing of 20 minutes each is enforced for English, Quant, and Reasoning. Negative marking of 0.25 marks per wrong answer.

questions.stem:
Rearrange the following six sentences (A) — (F) in the proper sequence to form a meaningful paragraph; then answer: which sentence will be the SECOND in the rearranged paragraph?

(A) Such collaborations have already produced affordable solar-roof installations in three states.
(B) The coming decade will demand a careful balance between economic growth and climate goals.
(C) Public-private partnerships are emerging as one practical model to deliver this balance.
(D) For India, this is not a distant problem — water stress and heat waves already shape daily life.
(E) Critics, however, warn that scale will determine whether the model can move the needle.
(F) The final test will be whether such partnerships endure beyond pilot programmes.
questions.explanation: Logical order: B (general statement) → D (specific claim about India) → C (introduces solution) → A (concrete example) → E (critique) → F (final test). Second sentence is D.
questions.subject: ENGLISH

questions.stem:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

(A) Neither the manager / (B) nor the supervisors / (C) was informed / (D) about the change.
questions.explanation: With 'neither/nor' the verb agrees with the subject NEAREST to it. The nearest subject is 'supervisors' (plural), so the verb must be 'were informed', not 'was informed'.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

(A) The committee have / (B) reviewed every proposal / (C) before submitting / (D) its final report.
questions.explanation: 'Committee' acting as a single body takes a singular verb — and the cue 'its final report' (singular pronoun) confirms the body is treated as one. So 'has reviewed' is correct, not 'have reviewed'.

questions.stem: What is the regulatory mandate that distinguishes Small Finance Banks from traditional commercial banks?
questions.passage_context: The recent rise of small-finance banks (SFBs) in India has begun reshaping the rural credit landscape. Unlike traditional commercial banks, SFBs are mandated to extend at least 75 per cent of their lending to priority sectors — agriculture, small businesses, and weaker sections — and to keep at least half of their loans to ticket sizes below ₹25 lakh. This regulatory architecture is meant to channel capital to borrowers whom larger banks have historically overlooked. Initial results are encouraging: SFBs have doubled their loan books in just five years, with collection efficiency above 95 per cent in most quarters. Yet the model is not without strain. Operating costs remain high because rural lending requires dense branch networks and feet-on-ground recovery. Margins are squeezed further whenever the central bank tightens liquidity. Some analysts argue that SFBs should be allowed to convert into universal banks once they cross a threshold of net worth, freeing them from the priority-sector cap. Others caution that such conversions risk the very mission these institutions were chartered to fulfil. The policy challenge, then, is to balance commercial sustainability with the social objective of inclusion. If SFBs can prove that profit and purpose are compatible at scale, they could become the template for the next generation of community-focused banking in India.
options: They must lend at least 75% to priority sectors and keep half their loans below ₹25 lakh ticket size.
They are restricted to operating only in metropolitan areas.
They are exempted from RBI supervision.
They can lend only to large corporations.
questions.explanation: The passage states this directly in the second sentence.
questions.subject: ENGLISH

questions.stem: A and B together can complete a piece of work in 12 days. B alone can finish it in 30 days. In how many days can A alone complete the same work?
questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/12. B's rate = 1/30. A's rate = 1/12 − 1/30 = (5 − 2)/60 = 3/60 = 1/20. A alone takes 20 days.
questions.subject: QUANT

questions.stem: A train 180 m long crosses a pole in 9 seconds. How long will it take to cross a platform 300 m long at the same speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = 180/9 = 20 m/s. Distance to cross platform = 180 + 300 = 480 m. Time = 480/20 = 24 s.
questions.subject: QUANT

questions.stem: A boat travels 30 km downstream in 2 hours and the same distance upstream in 3 hours. Find the speed of the stream.
questions.explanation: Downstream speed = 30/2 = 15 km/h. Upstream speed = 30/3 = 10 km/h. Speed of stream = (15 − 10)/2 = 2.5 km/h.
questions.subject: QUANT

questions.stem: The area of a rectangle is 168 sq. cm. If its length is 14 cm, find its perimeter.
questions.explanation: Width = 168/14 = 12 cm. Perimeter = 2(14 + 12) = 52 cm.

questions.stem: The radius of a circle is increased by 50%. By what percentage does its area increase?
questions.explanation: New radius = 1.5r. New area = π(1.5r)² = 2.25πr² = 2.25 × original area. Increase = 1.25 × original = 125%.

questions.stem: The average age of a class of 30 students is 14 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average rises to 15 years. Find the teacher's age.
questions.explanation: Total class age = 30 × 14 = 420. With teacher: 31 × 15 = 465. Teacher's age = 465 − 420 = 45.

questions.stem: The average weight of 9 men decreases by 1 kg when one man weighing 80 kg is replaced by another. What is the weight of the new man?

questions.stem: A bag contains coins of ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 denominations in the ratio 3:5:2. The total value is ₹460. Find the number of ₹2 coins.

questions.stem: Who sits at the immediate right of P?
questions.passage_context:
Eight friends — P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W — are seated in a single row, all facing North.
• T sits at one of the ends. Two persons sit between T and Q.
• R sits to the immediate right of Q. P sits to the immediate right of R.
• W sits to the immediate right of P. Three persons sit between W and U.
• S sits to the immediate left of U. V is not adjacent to T.
questions.explanation: P is at position 6, position 7 is W. So W sits to the immediate right of P.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: How many persons sit between Q and W?
questions.passage_context:
Eight friends — P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W — are seated in a single row, all facing North.
• T sits at one of the ends. Two persons sit between T and Q.
• R sits to the immediate right of Q. P sits to the immediate right of R.
• W sits to the immediate right of P. Three persons sit between W and U.
• S sits to the immediate left of U. V is not adjacent to T.
questions.explanation: Q is at position 4 and W is at position 7. Between them: positions 5 (R) and 6 (P) — two persons.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: Who sits at the extreme right end?

Eight friends — P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W — are seated in a single row, all facing North.

• W sits to the immediate right of P. Three persons sit between W and U.
• S sits to the immediate left of U. V is not adjacent to T.
questions.explanation: Position 8 is V.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs sit adjacent to each other?
questions.passage_context:
Eight friends — P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W — are seated in a single row, all facing North.
• T sits at one of the ends. Two persons sit between T and Q.
• R sits to the immediate right of Q. P sits to the immediate right of R.
• W sits to the immediate right of P. Three persons sit between W and U.
• S sits to the immediate left of U. V is not adjacent to T.
questions.explanation: S is at position 2 and U is at position 3 — they are adjacent. The other pairs are not.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: If S and V exchange positions, who sits to the immediate left of T?
questions.passage_context:
Eight friends — P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W — are seated in a single row, all facing North.
• T sits at one of the ends. Two persons sit between T and Q.
• R sits to the immediate right of Q. P sits to the immediate right of R.
• W sits to the immediate right of P. Three persons sit between W and U.
• S sits to the immediate left of U. V is not adjacent to T.
options: No one — T remains at the end
questions.explanation: T is at position 1 (extreme left end). No one sits to its left, regardless of any exchange.

questions.stem: Who sits to the immediate left of A?
questions.passage_context:
Six persons — A, B, C, D, E, and F — sit around a circular table facing the centre.
• A sits opposite D.
• B sits second to the right of A.
• C is to the immediate right of D.
• E sits between A and B.
• F occupies the only remaining seat.
questions.explanation: Convention: 'left' = anti-clockwise. A is at seat 1; anti-clockwise = seat 6 = F.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: Who sits opposite C?
questions.passage_context:
Six persons — A, B, C, D, E, and F — sit around a circular table facing the centre.
• A sits opposite D.
• B sits second to the right of A.
• C is to the immediate right of D.
• E sits between A and B.
• F occupies the only remaining seat.
questions.explanation: C is at seat 5. Opposite seat = (5+3) mod 6 = 2. Seat 2 = E.

questions.stem: How many persons sit between B and F when counted clockwise from B?

questions.stem: Which pair sits adjacent to each other?

Six persons — A, B, C, D, E, and F — sit around a circular table facing the centre.
• A sits opposite D.

questions.stem: Who lives on the topmost floor?

Five people — P, Q, R, S, and T — live on a 5-storey building, with the ground floor numbered 1 and the top floor numbered 5. Each lives on a different floor.

questions.stem: On which floor does R live?
questions.passage_context:
Five people — P, Q, R, S, and T — live on a 5-storey building, with the ground floor numbered 1 and the top floor numbered 5. Each lives on a different floor.
• P lives on floor 4.

questions.stem: How many floors are between Q and S?

Five people — P, Q, R, S, and T — live on a 5-storey building, with the ground floor numbered 1 and the top floor numbered 5. Each lives on a different floor.
• P lives on floor 4.
• Q lives immediately above S.
• T lives on an odd-numbered floor that is not the ground floor.

• P lives on floor 4.
• Q lives immediately above S.

questions.stem: Who is the youngest among the five friends?
questions.passage_context:
Five friends — A, B, C, D, and E — were each born in a different month: January, March, May, July, and September. The friend born in September is the youngest.

• Neither B nor C was born in May.

questions.stem: In which month was C born?

Five friends — A, B, C, D, and E — were each born in a different month: January, March, May, July, and September. The friend born in September is the youngest.
• A was born exactly two months before C.
• B was born after E but before D.

questions.stem: How many friends were born BEFORE B?
questions.passage_context:
Five friends — A, B, C, D, and E — were each born in a different month: January, March, May, July, and September. The friend born in September is the youngest.
• A was born exactly two months before C.
• B was born after E but before D.

questions.stem:
Statements: All cats are pets. Some pets are dogs. No dog is wild.
Conclusions:
I. Some pets are not wild.
II. All cats being wild is a possibility.
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Both Conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
I. Some pets are dogs and no dog is wild ⟹ those pets are not wild ⟹ some pets are not wild. FOLLOWS.
II. Cats are pets, but cats are not necessarily dogs (which are not-wild). The statements don't forbid cats from being wild, so the possibility holds. FOLLOWS.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
Statements: Some pens are pencils. All pencils are erasers. No eraser is sharpener.
Conclusions:
I. Some pens are erasers.
II. No pencil is sharpener.
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Both Conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
I. Some pens are pencils + all pencils are erasers ⟹ those pens are erasers ⟹ some pens are erasers. FOLLOWS.
II. All pencils are erasers + no eraser is sharpener ⟹ no pencil is sharpener. FOLLOWS.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
Statements: All books are novels. Some novels are stories. All stories are tales.
Conclusions:
I. All books are tales.
II. Some books being stories is a possibility.
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Both Conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
I. Books are novels, but only SOME novels are stories. Those books that are not in the story-overlap may not be tales. So we cannot conclude all books are tales. DOES NOT FOLLOW.
II. Possibility — it is consistent that all books fall in the novels-stories overlap (which are tales). POSSIBILITY HOLDS. FOLLOWS.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
Statements: All apples are fruits. No fruit is vegetable. Some vegetables are roots.
Conclusions:
I. No apple is vegetable.
II. Some apples are roots.
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Both Conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
I. All apples are fruits + no fruit is vegetable ⟹ no apple is vegetable. FOLLOWS.
II. The vegetable-root overlap doesn't connect to apples, and from I we know apples and vegetables are disjoint. So we cannot conclude any apples are roots. DOES NOT FOLLOW.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: Pointing to a man in a photograph, Riya said, 'He is the only son of my mother's father.' How is the man related to Riya's father?
questions.explanation: Riya's mother's father = Riya's maternal grandfather. The only son of this man = Riya's mother's brother = Riya's maternal uncle. The maternal uncle is Riya's father's brother-in-law (her father married his sister).
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: If A is the brother of B, B is the sister of C, and C is the father of D, how is A related to D?
questions.explanation: A and B are siblings; B and C are siblings — so A, B, C are all siblings. C is D's father, so D is C's child. A (a sibling of D's parent) is D's uncle.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: M is the wife of P. P is the only son of N. N has two daughters Q and R. R is married to S. T is the son of S. How is T related to M?
questions.explanation: P is M's husband and N's only son ⟹ N is M's father-in-law. N's daughter R = P's sister = M's sister-in-law. R married S; T is their son. So T is the son of M's sister-in-law ⟹ T is M's nephew.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: Aman walks 9 m east, then turns left and walks 12 m, then stops. How far is he from his starting point and in which direction?
questions.explanation: Net east = 9 m, net north = 12 m. Distance = √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 m. Direction: north-east (since both displacements are positive in N and E).
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: Pratima walks 5 km west, then 12 km south, then 13 km in the direction of her starting point. How far is she from her starting point now?
questions.explanation: After 5 km west and 12 km south, she's √(25+144) = 13 km from start (south-west). Walking 13 km in the direction of the starting point brings her exactly back to start. Distance = 0 km.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: A man walks 4 km north, then 3 km east, then 4 km south, then 3 km west. Where does he end up?
questions.explanation: Net: 4N − 4S = 0 north; 3E − 3W = 0 east. He returns to the starting point.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: In a code language, 'BANK' is written as 'EDQN'. How is 'LOAN' written in the same code?
questions.explanation: Each letter shifts +3: B→E, A→D, N→Q, K→N. Apply to LOAN: L→O, O→R, A→D, N→Q ⟹ ORDQ.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: In a code, 'PROFIT' is written as '7654321' — wait, let me redo. In a code, the first letter is replaced by its alphabet-position number. If 'CAT' = '3 1 20', then 'DOG' = ?
questions.explanation: Alphabet positions: D=4, O=15, G=7. So 'DOG' = '4 15 7'.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: In a code, 'TABLE' is written as 'GZYOV'. How is 'CHAIR' written in the same code?
questions.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its mirror in the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, etc., i.e. position 27−n). T(20)→G(7) ✓ since 27−20=7. Apply to CHAIR: C(3)→X(24), H(8)→S(19), A(1)→Z(26), I(9)→R(18), R(18)→I(9) ⟹ XSZRI.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
Statements: A > B ≤ C; B ≥ D > E; F = D < G
Conclusions:
I. A > E
II. F < C
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Both Conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
I. A > B ≥ D > E ⟹ A > E. FOLLOWS.
II. F = D ≤ B ≤ C ⟹ F ≤ C, with equality possible (e.g. D=B=C). So 'F < C' is not strictly guaranteed. DOES NOT FOLLOW.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
Statements: P ≥ Q < R = S; T > S ≥ U; V = U < W
Conclusions:
I. T > V
II. W > P
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Both Conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
I. T > S ≥ U = V ⟹ T > V. FOLLOWS.
II. W > V = U ≤ S, but P ≥ Q < R = S, so we can't determine W vs P. DOES NOT FOLLOW.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
Statements: K < L = M ≤ N; O > N; P ≥ M
Conclusions:
I. O > L
II. P > K
options: Either Conclusion I or II follows
Neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Both Conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
I. O > N ≥ M = L ⟹ O > L. FOLLOWS.
II. P ≥ M = L > K ⟹ P > K. FOLLOWS.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
In a class of 40 students, what is the average age?
I. The total age of all 40 students is 580 years.
II. The average age of the boys is 15 years and that of the girls is 14 years.
options: Either I or II alone is sufficient.
Neither I nor II is sufficient.
Both I and II are needed.
questions.explanation:
From I: average = 580/40 = 14.5 years. ✓ Sufficient.
From II: we don't know how many boys vs girls, so can't compute the overall average.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
How is M related to N?
I. M is the brother of P, who is the daughter of N's mother.
II. N is the only son of P's grandmother.
options: Either I or II alone is sufficient.
Neither I nor II is sufficient.
Both I and II are needed.
questions.explanation:
From I: M is brother of P, P is N's mother's daughter. So P is N's sister or N herself (if N's mother has only one daughter). Doesn't unambiguously tell M vs N.
From II: N is the only son of P's grandmother. P's grandmother could be N's mother, making N P's uncle. But which side?
Together: still ambiguous about whether N is on maternal or paternal side. Neither alone or together gives a clear relation.
questions.subject: REASONING
